description:
We are a passionate and ambitious team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge with our project THE LAST FOOTPRINT.

We are interested in space exploration, technology, scientific research, and creative problem-solving. We aim to combine our ideas and skills to develop an innovative project that highlights human impact on Mars and the importance of preserving its environment.

We believe in teamwork, creativity, and continuous learning, and we welcome people who are passionate.
summary:
We developed The Last Footprint, an interactive 3D web story for students aged 10–15 about three NASA rovers that completed their missions and remain silent on Mars: Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity. Students receive a signal from Mars, choose a landing site with SOL, a friendly guide robot, and wake each rover with a "Power Pulse". Each rover then tells its real story, with every line labelled Fact (checked against NASA sources) or Story. An Immersive Expedition lets students relive Spirit's real 2003–2004 journey, from launch to parachute and airbag landing.

This answers the "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge by turning retired hardware into characters children care about, showing that a finished mission still matters: its discoveries lead directly to Curiosity and Perseverance, which the story connects at the end.

It matters because it makes NASA history active and memorable, teaches students to separate fact from fiction, and is fully bilingual in Arabic and English, bringing interactive space science to Arabic-speaking children. It runs free in any browser, on phones and school computers, even offline.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

The Last Footprint is an interactive 3D story that runs in any web browser. It brings three NASA rovers that completed their missions and remain on Mars (Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity) back to life for students aged 10–15.

1. Receive the signal: Mars appears in 3D, lit by the Sun exactly as it is right now (computed live with NASA's Mars24 algorithm). A live counter shows how long Spirit has been silent since its last contact on 22 March 2010.

2. Choose a path: "Instant Warp" (about 2 minutes) lets students pick one of the three real landing sites with SOL, a friendly guide robot, and dive to the surface. "Immersive Expedition" (about 5 minutes) lets them live Spirit's real journey: launch from Cape Canaveral on 10 June 2003, a 7-month, 487-million-km cruise, atmospheric entry at about 19,000 km/h, the parachute at about 10 km, airbags about 8 seconds before touchdown, and about 30 bounces across Mars, all controlled by the student.

3. Wake the rovers: in the Rover Hall, students hold a "Power Pulse" to send energy to a sleeping, dusty rover. It wakes up and tells its story. Every line is labelled Fact (checked against NASA sources) or Story (our fiction).

4. Explore: real mission timelines, Earth photographed by Spirit from Mars (PIA05547), a game to save Spirit from its real Sol-18 memory crisis, a fact-or-myth quiz about Opportunity's "last words", and a side-by-side comparison of the three rovers.

5. The Next Footprint: a trail links the three rovers to Curiosity and Perseverance, still working today. Students write their name and download a Mars Explorer certificate.

HOW IT WORKS

A single web page built with three.js (WebGL). It uses NASA's 3D Mars Exploration Rover model, Mars and Earth texture maps, live Sun position from Mars24, a post-processing chain (bloom, colour grading, film grain), real-time sound design with the Web Audio API, and recorded Microsoft Azure neural voices for SOL and the rovers in Arabic and English. It needs no server, no accounts and no tracking, and runs offline.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Students learn real space history through action, not reading: why missions outlast their plans, how a rover lands, and how engineers solve problems from millions of kilometres away. The Fact/Story labels teach critical thinking and source checking. A built-in 20-minute lesson plan with discussion questions helps teachers use it in class. Because it is fully bilingual, it brings interactive NASA science to Arabic-speaking children, who rarely get such content in their own language. Our goal is that every student leaves knowing that a mission may end, but its footprint remains.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

JavaScript (three.js r186, Web Audio API, Canvas), HTML and CSS, esbuild; Microsoft Azure AI Speech and ffmpeg for the character voices; Python and Playwright for automated testing (features, accessibility with axe-core, offline and memory tests); GitHub Pages for hosting. No special hardware is needed.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Instead of presenting "abandoned" rovers as dead machines, we turned them into characters that students wake up and listen to. The student does not just read about landing on Mars; they launch, steer through entry, open the parachute and inflate the airbags themselves. Real NASA data drives the experience: the Sun on Mars is in its true position at the moment the student plays.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Accuracy: every Fact line is checked against NASA and JPL sources, and fiction is always labelled.

- Age 10–15: short lines, clear goals, hands-on interaction, a reward at the end.

- Language: full Arabic and English, including voices and right-to-left layout.

- Access: works on phones and ordinary school computers, offline, with keyboard play, screen-reader labels, a reduced-motion mode and WCAG 2.1 AA checks.

- Privacy and safety: no accounts, no data collected; all NASA images are credited and no AI image is presented as real.
